en: In the *Jingtu jue* (Decisions on the Pure Land), the former editor, Li Zhuowu of Wenling, cited the Great Being Vimalakīrti, who said: "As one's mind is pure, so is the Buddha-land pure.
The Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) of Amitābha Buddha is the purity of that land. To recite the name of Amitābha Buddha and [visualize] the Land of Ultimate Bliss...

The "land" is the purity of the mind. To recollect Amitābha Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss and thereby be born in Amitābha Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss is because, as the mind is pure, so too is the Buddha-land pure. Thus, for one who recollects the Buddha:
One contemplates this Pure Land. Those who practice Zen also contemplate this Pure Land. How, then, can they be distinguished?
Therefore, those who recite the Buddha's name will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land. As for those who practice Zen, how could they possibly abandon this Pure Land to go elsewhere?
If they were to go elsewhere, that would be two lands; it would not be pure. Amitābha...
The Buddha’s Land of Ultimate Bliss cannot tolerate such things. For those who practice *chan* (meditation), it goes without saying that they do not depend on rebirth there;
yet for those who practice *nianfo* (recitation of the Buddha's name), how could they wait until they have gone somewhere before being born?

If one must wait until they have gone somewhere before being born, then this would mean that by reciting the Buddha's name here one goes there, and by reciting my name there I come here—a process of one coming and one going.
The former [two] are also two lands; they are not pure. The Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha cannot tolerate such things either.
Therefore, one should know that the Pure Land of Amitābha Buddha is precisely the Pure Land of one's own mind. Recite the Buddha’s name and practice Zen meditation.
This is precisely the means by which one purifies one's own mind. I therefore exhort all students: do not look down upon Zen practitioners while looking lightly upon the Pure Land.
Thus, I have collected the words of various supreme sages who exhorted people to practice the Pure Land, and combined them to form this "Resolution on the Pure Land."
Preface to the *Jingtu jueyi* (Decisions on Doubts Concerning the Pure Land),
compiled by the Tiantai Master Zhizhe: *The Ten Doubts Regarding the Pure Land*.
Preface to the *Ten Doubts* by the Layman Wúwéi of the Song Dynasty;
"The Three Contemplations in One Mind" by Chan Master Shòu, Exhorting the Practice of Pure Land Devotion;
and "Answers to Questions" by Xíngjiǎo Qísī Zōngběn.
The Three Great Sages Manifesting Themselves to Encourage Practice;
Scriptures and Treatises Pointing to the Pure Land; Patriarchs Pointing to the Western Quarter;
Verses of Praise for the Western Quarter; The Five Invocations to the West.
The Eight Verses on the Recitation of the Buddha’s Name:
A Resolution of Doubts Concerning the Pure Land by the Tiantai Master Zhiyi, from the *Ten Doubts about the Pure Land*.
Preface to the *Ten Doubts Regarding the Pure Land* by the Song Dynasty Layman Yang Jie, Wuming.
The Chan Master of Wenling said:
"The Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation cannot be practiced by relying solely on phenomenal appearances (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*). The Buddha possesses the three [bodies]."

Regarding the body: maintain mindfulness of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) in order to destroy the three delusions (*trivisa*). Only then can one enter the stage of the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). To maintain mindfulness of the three contemplations is as follows:

for instance, upon uttering the name of a Buddha, one realizes that the essence of this act of recollecting is empty (*śūnya*), and that the object of recollection is signless (*animitta*). This is maintaining mindfulness of the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*).

The Buddha who is the object of recollection is the *saṃbhoga-kāya* (reward-body); this is the mind destroying the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *saṃjñā-kleśa*). Although it is the subject that recollects...
The essence is empty; that which is contemplated is signless (*animitta*). This does not hinder the clarity of the contemplating mind nor the manifest appearance of that which is contemplated.

Thus, while the contemplation exists, it is a provisional observation (*prajñā-vipaśyanā*); the Buddha who is the object of contemplation is the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). This is precisely the mind breaking through the sands of delusion.

At the very moment when both the contemplating subject and the contemplated object are empty, they are simultaneously manifest; at the very moment when both the contemplating subject and the contemplated object are manifest, this is precisely [the realization of emptiness].

The subject of mindfulness and the object of mindfulness are quiescent; emptiness and the provisional exist in mutual dependence. This is precisely the Middle Way contemplation within the state where mindfulness abides.

The Buddha who is the object of mindfulness is none other than the Dharmakāya; it is the very mind that shatters the delusions of ignorance. When explained in this way, the practitioner’s application of the mind consists solely in one true thought;
there is no further distinction to be made.
The Monk Zhuowu said: "Tiantai Zhiyi’s *Ten Treatises on Resolving Doubts* may truly be called a bridge for rebirth in the Pure Land.
How could later students have any further doubts? The layman Yang Wuweishi of the Song dynasty wrote a preface for it, praising those who recite the Buddha's name as being certain to attain rebirth;
this, too, is one way of resolving doubts. — From the *Wenling Fa...* [Note: The source text appears to be truncated.]

The Master further elucidated the principle of the threefold contemplation within one mind (*ekacitta-trivipaśyanā*). He praised those who practice *nienfo* (Buddha-recollection), stating that they will certainly behold the Buddha;

this was yet another resolution of doubts. Viewing these points together, one then understands that the principles of Tiantai’s Pure Land *zhiguan* (calming and contemplation) are nothing other than the revelation of this Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*), so that students may know that the very arising of a thought brings forth rebirth [in the Pure Land].
In the Pure Land, one beholds the Buddha upon opening the mouth, without waiting for the toil of rebirth.
What doubt, then, can there be regarding rebirth—why not for a single thought-moment recite "Namu Amida Butsu"?
When a person of the Song dynasty wished to study ancient prose but could not, the Layman Wuwei was able to do so spontaneously without studying; his literary style was sublime.
Excellent! This further demonstrates that those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha have nowhere they go that does not rely upon the power of the Buddha.
It would be well for each of you to apply yourselves with diligence to mindfulness of the Buddha.
This is Master Shou’s exhortation to cultivate the Pure Land practice (as seen in the *Wanshan tonggui ji*).
Question: Regarding the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha while walking (*cankrama*) versus mindfulness while sitting (*niṣadyā*), how do they compare?

Answer: It is like sailing with the wind against the current; one might still say that progress is being made. Yet, if one sails with the wind while following the current, the speed is easily understood.

A single recitation while sitting can already eliminate the sins of eighty billion kalpas; as for the merit of reciting while walking, how could one know its measure? Thus, it is said in a sutra: [The merit of walking while reciting is immeasurable].

If one practices the Way five hundred times and recites the Buddha’s name one thousand times, such as these deeds are constantly performed, the Buddha of the Western Land will naturally manifest before one.
[Question: If the Pure Land of the Mind alone pervades the ten directions, how can it be that one entrusts one's substance to the lotus pedestal and lodges one's form in An-yang (Sukhāvatī)? And...
If one gives rise to thoughts of acceptance and rejection, how can one reach the gate of non-arising? If feelings of delight and aversion arise, how can one achieve equanimity? Answer:
Regarding the Buddha-land as mind-only, it arises only when the mind is fully understood. As the *Tathāgata-acintya-viṣaya-sūtra* states:
"All Buddhas of the three periods of time are non-existent; they exist solely in dependence upon their own minds. If a Bodhisattva is able to understand all...

The Buddha and all phenomena are merely the measure of the mind. Upon attaining the patience that accords with reality (*anulomikī-kṣānti*), one either enters the first stage (*prathamā bhūmi*) and, after casting off the body, is swiftly reborn in the world of Abhirati, or is born within the pure buddha-field of Sukhāvatī. Therefore, know that it is only when the mind is purified that the Pure Land of Mind-Only arises;
to cling to objects is merely to fall back into the realm of objective conditions. As stated in the Sūtra: "If a person focuses their mindfulness..."
The roots of goodness cultivated by Amitābha Buddha in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss are dedicated toward the vow to seek rebirth in that world;
one will immediately attain rebirth there. Because one constantly beholds the Buddha, there shall never be any falling back.

*Qunyi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts). Question: "The lands of all Buddhas are likewise entirely empty. One contemplates sentient beings as being like a 'fifth great element' [which does not exist].
How can one grasp at the existence of marks, abandoning this life to be born in that? Answer:

"You merely see the teachings explaining the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature) as being without marks, and the passages refuting the *parikalpita-svabhāva* (imagined nature) as being ultimately empty and non-existent; you do not believe the explanations regarding the *paratantra-svabhāva* (dependent nature)."

Those who teach the doctrine of arising through the causes and conditions of nature are people who do not believe in cause and effect; they speak of the characteristic of the total annihilation of all phenomena.
Thus, a verse from the Avataṃsaka Sūtra says:
Question: One would rather undergo all manner of suffering throughout immeasurable eons than ever distance oneself from the Tathāgata or fail to behold his sovereign power.
[The interlocutor asks: Since there are no phenomena external to the mind and the Buddha neither comes nor goes, how can there be such things as seeing the Buddha or being welcomed by him? Answer:

Mind-only buddha-remembrance: through the contemplation of mind-only, it universally encompasses all phenomena. Having realized that objects are mind-only, one realizes that the mind is itself the Buddha;
therefore, whatever one contemplates is none other than the Buddha. The *Prajñāsamādhi Sūtra* says: "It is like a person who dreams of the seven treasures and their kinsmen rejoicing;
upon waking, they long for them but do not know where they are. Such is the way of buddha-remembrance. This is the analogy.
It is produced solely by the mind; thus, while existing, it is empty, and therefore there is no coming or going. Furthermore, as an illusion is not real, both mind and Buddha are absent;
yet, because illusory appearances are not non-existent, mind and Buddha are not destroyed. When emptiness and existence are without obstruction, there is neither going nor coming.

It is not an obstacle to universal vision. According to various sutras, those born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) possess powerful conditions and an excellent realm; their merit is complete and their lifespan long.
They are born by transformation within lotus flowers and are personally welcomed by the Buddha, whereupon they ascend to the rank of Bodhi.

Born into the family of the Tathāgata, they abide in the gate of non-retrogression (avaivartika), receive the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa), and their bodies are endowed with radiant light and wondrous marks. Their footsteps tread upon jeweled trees and fragrances.
On the altar, offerings are presented to the ten directions, and the spirit is settled in samādhi. Constantly reaching the ears is the Dharma of the Mahāyāna;

those standing shoulder-to-shoulder are all persons neighboring the stage of *abhiṣeka* (the place of succession). Every thought is empty and profound; every mind is in tranquil contemplation. The flames of affliction are extinguished, and the springs of craving and desire run dry.
Since even the name of the evil realms no longer exists, how could there be any matter of saṃsāra? The *Anguo Chao* says: "That which is called the ultimate..."
Regarding "joy," there are twenty-four kinds of joy. The *Qun yi lun* (Treatise on Resolving Doubts) states: "In the Pure Land of the West, there are thirty kinds of benefit.
Why then do you sink and drown without concern amidst the waves and depths of the river of desire? Why do you burn without fear within the blazing flames of the house on fire?

Furthermore, as long as you have not shed this karmic body, you will ultimately remain entangled by the three obstacles. Since you do not cherish the transformed form upon the lotus throne, you must instead receive birth from a womb."
Regarding form: if one receives a physical body, the entire body is suffering. Having sunk into the three realms, how can one avoid the cycle of *saṃsāra*?
Thus, the *Maudgalyāyana-paripṛcchā-sūtra* states: The Buddha told Maudgalyāyana, "It is like ten thousand rivers flowing continuously;

there are floating plants and wood that do not look back at what is behind nor look forward at what is ahead, yet they all converge in the great ocean. The world is also like this: although there may be nobility, wealth, and pleasure,"

No one can escape birth, old age, sickness, and death. It is solely because they do not believe in the Buddhist scriptures that, when they become humans in future lives, they will suffer even greater hardship and distress, unable to be born in the lands of the thousand Buddhas.

For this reason, I have said that the land of the Buddha of Infinite Life is easy to reach and easy to be born in; yet people cannot believe it deeply, instead serving the ninety-six kinds of heterodox paths.
I say that such a person is called one without eyes; they are called one without ears.
Question: Master Pang said, "To speak of the Buddha-land in terms of affairs, it is a hundred thousand li away; the great ocean is vast and boundless."
As soon as there is movement, the black wind arises. Though those who set out may number in the thousands, those who reach their destination are not even one or two in ten thousand.

When suddenly encountering the person of original nature, one is no longer within the realm of causes and conditions. How can this be understood and realized so as to attain rebirth? Answer: If one extracts the essential principle and examines the root, [it is as follows].

Since one does not even speak of the existence of a Buddha or a land, how could one discuss whether there is realization or non-realization? Thus, the celestial truth is inherently complete and does not depend on causes and conditions;
it does not stir so much as a hair’s breadth and is eternally in profound accord with the true essence. If discussed in terms of phenomena, however, they are certainly not uniform.

Regarding rebirth in the nine grades, those at both the upper and lower levels reach their destination. Some may travel to the Land of Transformation to behold the Buddha’s response-body (nirmāṇakāya), while others are born in the Land of Retribution to perceive the Buddha’s true body (dharmakāya).
Some may ascend to the higher stages in a single night, while others may require the passage of kalpas before they realize the Lesser Vehicle.

Whether of sharp or dull faculties, with concentrated or distracted minds, or with varying speeds of awakening—since their capacities differ, or whether the flowers bloom early or late, since their temporal limits vary—these are fully recorded from ancient times to the present.
They arise together among both ordinary beings and sages; the manifestations of these phenomena are clearly evident.
This is clearly evidenced by direct observation; thus, Śākyamuni Buddha personally recorded that Mañjuśrī would be born in the land of Amitābha Buddha and attain the first bhūmi.
A Great Sūtra states: Maitreya Bodhisattva asked the Buddha, "I do not yet know how many non-retrogressive bodhisattvas in this world-system will be able to be born in that land.
The Buddha replied, "In this Sahā world, there are six thousand seven hundred million [such bodhisattvas]."
Bodhisattvas who do not regress shall all attain rebirth there. Throughout his life, the Great Master Zhiwei cultivated the practices for the Western Land;

all the merits and wisdom he accumulated for the two adornments were dedicated toward that goal. At the time of his death, together with his disciples, he chanted the names of the sixteen contemplations and, joining his palms in praise, said:
"The forty-eight vows adorn the Pure Land; its fragrant terraces and jeweled trees are easy to reach, yet no one goes there."

When the signs of the iron-wheeled chariot hell appear, even those who repent for a single thought will still attain rebirth; how much more so for those who cultivate through precepts, concentration, and wisdom, and who practice the Path with great vigor—their efforts shall never be in vain.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states that the Buddhas of the ten directions, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, [bear witness to this].
He extends his broad and long tongue, which completely covers the great trichiliocosm. Having realized the non-arising of phenomena, how could this be a mere fabrication? Question:

The *Contemplation Sūtra* clarifies that the sixteen gates of contemplation all involve concentrating the mind to cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*). One must contemplate the Buddha’s marks and signs until they are clearly and perfectly understood before one can ascend to the Pure Land.
How, then, can those with a distracted mind be transformed and sent there? Answer: Regarding the textual passages on the nine grades [of rebirth]:...

There is naturally ascent and descent; the upper and lower realms encompass all, yet they do not transcend two states of mind: first, the concentrated mind, as when one cultivates meditative absorption and practices contemplation;

second, the single-minded mind, which consists solely in reciting the name while dedicating the merit and making vows. Indeed, there are the two wheels of good and evil, and the two retributions of suffering and joy.
All are created by the three karmas, produced by the four conditions, accomplished by common causes, and subsumed within the five fruits.

If the mind is pure, one is born through transformation in a pure land of fragrant terraces and jeweled trees; if the mind is defiled, one receives birth in a foul land of hills, mounds, pits, and ravines.
All these are fruits of equal status that can evoke superior conditions. Therefore, apart from the source of one’s own mind, there is no separate entity.
The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "For example, like a precious king of jewels, various colors appear according to the mind;
because the minds of sentient beings are pure, they perceive pure lands. The *Mahāsaṃnipāta Sūtra* says: "If you wish to purify your realm, simply purify your own mind. Thus, we know this.
All things return to the mind; the myriad dharmas arise from me. If you wish to attain the pure realm, simply practice the pure causes.
Just as the nature of water is to flow downward and the nature of fire is to ascend, such is the force of these principles; what cause for doubt is there?
In the "Postscript on Encouraging Cultivation" for Chan Master Shou, Zhuowu wrote:

"When the Chan Master was still a minor official in Yuhang, he already diligently cultivated the Pure Land practice. Because of his diligent cultivation, he cherished all living beings and could not bear to kill them;
this is still merely in accordance with the honored teachings and admonitions of Buddhism. Yet, because he could not bear to kill, he consequently..."

It expanded until it reached the practice of releasing living beings. Because of this practice of releasing living beings, it further expanded until it reached the purchase of living beings for release.
Because of this purchase of living beings for release, it again expanded until it reached the embezzlement of funds by prison guards.

I purchase and release living beings; even if I were to commit a crime punishable by the ultimate penalty, I would accept it gladly. For one begins with an inability to bear the thought of killing, and this culminates in the point of committing suicide.
This is because one would rather take one's own life than fail to fulfill the original resolve of an inability to bear the thought of killing.

This is what he aspired to. Although his aim was unsuitable from the perspective of principle and impossible given the circumstances, observing his aspiration, one cannot say that he did not have deep faith in the practice of *śubhakarmā* (pure deeds).
Now, abstaining from killing is but a single thought-moment of the Buddha and merely one matter among the many practices of cultivation;
yet even this is treated with such gravity, so the rest may be inferred. Thus it is...
If one practices in this way, what task is there that cannot be accomplished? What merit is there that cannot be achieved? What Buddha is there that cannot be realized?
And what Amitābha is there that cannot be seen? In the highest grade of the highest birth, even the Lord Yama pays his respects.

This is indeed appropriate. Regarding the cultivation of the practice of purity (*śubha-karman*), there are fundamentally two gates: the gate of subduing (*nigraha*) and the gate of gathering (*saṃgraha*). Śākyamuni represents the gate of subduing, while Amitābha represents the gate of gathering.
Furthermore, there are two gates of aspiration and aversion (*abhinandanā* and *vidveṣa*): one solely feels aversion toward this life, and thus fears that one will not be able to relinquish it;
one solely aspires to that birth, and thus naturally beholds the Buddha without doubt. As for the fool, he says: [The text continues with the fool's objection.]
It is not permissible to fail to feel revulsion for this life.

Nor is it permissible to claim that one does not recognize the grace of the Buddhas in their methods of subduing and gathering beings through both sternness and kindness. Yet, when viewed from the perspective of a Zen master’s mind, I still find myself full of attachment.
It is simply that they have not abandoned [the practice]. You have been born into the superior grade; as for me, I do not know what grade I shall attain. Fortunately, there are but nine grades.

Even if there were hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, or billions of grades, would I not be the Buddha of the very lowest among those hundreds, thousands, ten thousands, millions, and billions?
This is something one must take as a warning. Therefore, those who cultivate the practice of Pure Land must resolutely—
One must not fail to take Chan Master Shou as one's model and me, the old man Li Zhuowu, as a mirror, thereby admonishing oneself.
However, I alone am unable to admonish myself; for this reason, I respectfully record these words of exhortation to practice, so that I may observe and reflect upon them from time to time.
I shall continue to serve Chan Master [Shou] and the Tiantai master Zhiyi in the upper hall, hoping that—
Although I cannot compare even to a ten-thousandth part of the two masters,
I may perhaps equal Lord Yan’s practice of prostrating and taking refuge morning and evening. Furthermore, I wish that every person would, like Lord Yan,
respectfully pay homage to the images, burn incense, and read this book at dawn.
According to his biography, Master Shou was a native of Danyang. He had originally served as a clerk in Yuhang County.

Having squandered nearly all the funds from the treasury, the authorities investigated him; it turned out he had used the money solely for the purchase of living beings to be released. His crime merited death. As he faced execution, his countenance remained serene and joyful.
Turning to the prison official, he said, "In my lifetime, I have released tens of millions of living beings. Now that I am about to die..."
He returned directly to the Western Land; how joyful this was! When the King of Qian heard of this, he marveled at him, released him from his punishment, and he subsequently became a monk.
He dreamed that Avalokiteśvara poured nectar into his mouth. He resided at Yongming Temple until the age of ninety-eight, whereupon he sat in meditation and passed away with palms joined.
He was interred beneath a stupa. A certain monk circumambulated the stupa and prostrated there every day. Someone asked him:

As for the reason, he replied: "I am a monk from Fuzhou. Once, while ill, I arrived at the Office of the Netherworld and saw a scroll of a painted image in a corner of the hall, which King Yama came daily to prostrate before.
I asked the presiding official, who said: 'This is Chan Master Shou of Yongming Temple in Hangzhou.
Of all those who die as humans, they must pass through this place; only Chan Master Shou does not. "
This person has already been reborn in the highest grade of the highest level in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss.
Because the King revered him, he depicted this image as an offering.
He traveled on foot to seek out a teacher (as recorded in the *Direct Pointing at the Source*).
Zongben asked, "I, your disciple, wish to escape birth and death, yet I do not know upon what dharma I should rely for cultivation.
The Chan Master praised him, saying, "Though your years are young, your resolve is lofty. Listen to what I say regarding the direct path to practice: simply recite the name of Amitābha Buddha.
Zongben said, "Ordinary people have many karmic offenses; how can one attain rebirth in the Pure Land by reciting the Buddha's name for only a single lifetime?"

[Question on] the Pure Land. Answer: The *Sutra of the Sixteen Contemplations* states: "To mindfully recite 'Namo Amitābha Buddha' with a sincere heart, a single utterance extinguishes the heavy sins of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas.

If there are those who have committed the five heinous crimes and the ten evil deeds throughout their lives, yet at the moment of death they recite the name of Amitābha Buddha ten times, they still attain rebirth;
how much more so for those who observe the precepts and recite the Buddha’s name throughout an entire lifetime? [Question:]
Question: For what reason does Amitābha Buddha possess such vast merit and vast vows? Answer: The *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra* states:
"When I attain Buddhahood, my fame shall transcend the ten directions; humans and devas shall joyfully hear it."
They all come to preside over my land; those in the realms of hell, hungry ghosts, and animals are likewise born within my land.
Thus, it can be known that there is no one within the three realms and the six paths of saṃsāra who is not saved.
Amitābha Buddha currently dwells in the Western World of Ultimate Bliss, and furthermore, throughout the worlds of the ten directions, he teaches and transforms countless devas and humans.
This extends even to the classes of creatures that flutter and wriggle. "Fluttering" refers to minute flying insects;
"wriggling" refers to minute crawling worms. If the Buddha still transforms and delivers such beings, how much more so those who are human?
Furthermore, Amitābha Buddha has another vow: "If one invokes my name and does not necessarily be born in my land, I shall not become a Buddha."
For this reason, they extensively deliver sentient beings without end; yet if a person takes refuge for even a single thought-moment, they shall be born in that land.
Inferring from this, the merit of recollecting the Buddha is truly inconceivable. It further says: "If there are sentient beings..."
Those who wish to be reborn in my land in the highest grade must employ a heart of compassion and refrain from killing;

they must cherish all sentient beings, maintain the various precepts, recite the Mahāyāna sūtras, understand the primary meaning, clearly comprehend the profound principle of reality, make offerings to the Triple Gem, show filial piety toward both parents, feel pity for those in poverty and suffering, and transform sentient beings.
If one can practice mindfulness of the Buddha in this manner, rebirth in the highest grade is certain.

One will be reborn in the higher realms and proceed directly until the attainment of Buddhahood. Should one’s strength be insufficient, one should simply maintain the precepts and fasts oneself, reciting the Buddha’s name with single-minded devotion.

If one can do so continuously, thought after thought, without interruption, one will not be reborn in the lower grade either. Moreover, this Dharma gate does not discriminate between the worthy and the foolish;
it does not select between the noble and the lowly; it does not depend on wealth or poverty; it makes no distinction between male and female; and it takes no account of old or young.
Whether monastic or lay, regardless of how long one has practiced or how recently, all may practice the mindfulness of the Buddha (*nien-fo*).

The rules for this mindfulness are likewise unrestricted: one may recite with a loud voice, a low voice, in a flowing chant, while prostrating, with a concentrated mind, through investigative inquiry, by encouraging others to remember, while turning a prayer bead rosary, while walking, while standing, while sitting quietly, while lying on one’s side, silently, or clearly.
A thousand thoughts and ten thousand thoughts are all but a single thought; the sole requirement is to resolve with firm faith to seek rebirth in the Pure Land.
If one can practice in this manner, what need is there to seek out other teachers? It may be said that the success of the boat depends entirely on the helmsman;

those who attain this shall together ascend to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang). Question: People of the world often say that they are entangled by domestic affairs and preoccupied with worldly duties.
[The interlocutor] replied: "I am bound by worldly entanglements. Let me wait until old age before I can practice the recitation of the Buddha's name. [The Master] answered: "How bitter! How bitter!

Have you not seen what Zen Master Sīcīn said? 'People of the world may have wealth and treasures as high as mountains and wives and concubines filling their rooms, enjoying themselves day and night.'"
How could he not desire to remain in this world for a long life? Yet, alas, one’s future destiny is limited; it presses from within in secret.
When the summons arrives, one must depart immediately, with no room for delay. The Old Man Yanluo does not follow human sentiment; what face would the King of Impermanence have?
Moreover, as you all have personally seen with your own eyes and heard with your own ears throughout the streets and alleys, among your own kinsmen...
One’s kinsmen, friends, brothers, and the vigor of one’s youth—how many such lifetimes have perished? Have you not heard the words of the ancients:
"Do not wait until old age to study the Way; the solitary graves are all those of the young. And it is further said:
"Since early years, seeking a wife and raising children, managing the household affairs, and enduring a myriad of bitter hardships, suddenly the three-inch breath is severed."

Before long, everything will come to an end. If one is a filial descendant, one might offer vegetarian feasts for several monks, read a few sections of the scriptures, burn some paper money, prepare a bowl of soup and rice on the third day of spring and the ninth day of autumn, and weep a few times;
yet these are merely acts of remembering one’s parents. As for the unworthy son, while his parents are still dead and their bones have not yet grown cold, he treats their estate as plundered wealth.
They sell off their fields and gardens to spend money on music and pleasure as they please. When compared to this, what is there to be so anxious about?
"Grandchildren have their own blessings; do not create distant anxieties for them. Furthermore, he quotes an ancient master:

"With a cold laugh at the wealthy old man, his livelihood is as frantic as a speeding arrow. Insects breed within his granaries; the strings of coins in his treasury rot. By day he holds the scale..."

[The Master] said: "Counting the nights by the lighting of lamps, this physical form is like a puppet; do not let its strings snap. To such an extent does he speak with bitter urgency, urging people toward the death-mind.
Have you ever been granted permission to merely pursue worldly affairs, waiting until old age before reciting the Buddha’s name?

You should reflect that there is but a short time for a human being to dwell in this world. Like sparks from a flint or a flash of lightning, it passes in the blink of an eye. Seize this moment while you are not yet old."
Before illness strikes, rouse both body and mind and cast aside worldly affairs. Seize a single day’s time to recite the Buddha’s name;

seize a single period of effort to cultivate pure karma. Thus, when the end of life arrives—whether it be a "good death" or a "bad death"—one need only ensure that one's provisions for the journey have been prepared in advance.
In this way, my own future path will be secure and steady.
This is clear. If you do not act accordingly, it will be difficult to remedy your regrets later. Moreover, this Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance can be practiced by all people.
It is like a dark room of a thousand years: a single lamp illuminating it brings light.
Therefore, even those who slaughter horses or butcher oxen can practice it simply by laying down their butcher’s knife. Thus, practicing is not difficult, nor does it hinder anything.
All worldly affairs: for those in office, it does not hinder their duties; for scholars, it does not hinder their studies; for merchants, it does not hinder their trade;
for farmers, it does not hinder their cultivation; for women, it does not hinder their domestic labors; for those in public offices, it does not hinder their service to superiors;
for monks, it does not hinder their Zen practice. In all that they do, none of these things interfere with one another.
[This practice] is not obstructed. Whether performed during morning or evening devotions, or finding leisure amidst busyness;
whether reciting a thousand or a hundred times, or five hundred or three hundred times, or even ten times—what is required is solely the dedication of merit and the making of vows.

If one can be sincere in this way, wishing for rebirth in the Western Land, one will certainly attain rebirth there. It is further said: "O son of good family, now, taking this single Dharma-realm..."

The Dharma is entrusted to you. As for the ten dharma-realms—namely, the Buddha-dharma realm, the Bodhisattva-dharma realm, the Pratyekabuddha-dharma realm, the Śrāvaka-dharma realm, the Deva-dharma realm, the Human-dharma realm, the Asura-dharma realm, the Preta-dharma realm, the Tiryagyoni-dharma realm, and the Naraka-dharma realm—the ten dharma-realms are fully present within a single mind.
One experiences them according to what one creates. This is based on...
The causes you have created are returned to you. The results of your actions—whether virtuous or non-virtuous conduct—are the causes of the mundane world.

The three realms and six paths of existence are the results of the mundane world. Upholding the precepts and reciting the Buddha’s name are the causes for transcending the mundane world. Attaining Buddhahood in the Pure Land is the result of transcending the mundane world.
On the path to the human and celestial realms, the cultivation of merit comes first; within the sea of birth and death, [recite the Buddha's name].

The Buddha is supreme. Now, there are those who desire happiness in the realms of humans and devas yet do not cultivate merit; those who wish to transcend birth and death yet do not practice mindfulness of the Buddha.
This is like a bird wishing to fly without wings, or a tree wishing to flourish without roots—how could such things be possible?
One must take mindfulness of the Buddha as the direct cause. Mindfulness of the Buddha now is the cause, and the moment of death is the fruit. To commit evil and then [expect a good result]...
When the objective realm manifests before one, by recollecting the Buddha, the fruit of Buddhahood arrives of its own accord. Does one not see that the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:

"If a person wishes to thoroughly know all Buddhas of the three periods of time, they should contemplate the nature of the Dharma-realm: everything is created solely by the mind"? This is precisely it.
Zongben replied to the question:
Someone may ask, "Worldly people each cling to their own public cases (gong'an), seeking only to practice Chan and realize the Way, while having no wish to be reborn in the Pure Land.
What do you think of this? He replied: "Practicing Chan does not obstruct reciting the Buddha's name; reciting the Buddha's name does not obstruct practicing Chan. Furthermore, as for going..."

Within the *Shenglu* (Records of Birth) and the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks), both the worthy and the foolish are recorded together; this has been so throughout past and present. Casting off the defiled lands, all shall proceed toward the Pure Land.
Conceived within the pools of the seven treasures, they abandon the suffering of the womb. Transcending ordinary beings and even sages, they attain the Way and realize the Truth.

Without passing through the three great kalpas, they immediately achieve Buddhahood. Is this not proof that the power of the Buddha is inconceivable? Therefore, those who wish to transcend birth and death—
Regarding the attainment of the bliss of nirvāṇa within saṃsāra, there is no dharma-gate for rebirth that surpasses this. Why is this?

In the turbid realm of Sahā, where all manner of suffering accumulates, it is difficult to accomplish the Way. In the joyful land of the Pure Land, where all virtues gather, one attains the stage of non-retrogression.
Those who invoke the Name are protected by the mindfulness of all Buddhas and attain rebirth; those who resolve upon Bodhicitta are illuminated by the light of Amitābha.
They continue to progress. Bodhisattvas and Arhats, along with their companions, the waterfowl, and the forest trees—all alike mindfully recollect the Buddha.
Their ears constantly hear the wondrous Dharma, and within their hearts, greed and anger are instantly severed. Their happiness is inexhaustible; what limit could there be to their lifespan?

Having been born in that land in a single lifetime, they immediately attain the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). How can this compare to the realms of humans and devas, where every turn of the eye encounters many conditions of both adversity and favor? [This is] expedient.

The roots of goodness cultivated along the path are rare and perfectly complete. Yet, even those in the three stages of worthiness prior to the grounds (*bhūmi*) may lose mindfulness before they have yet seen the Path;
those in the six abodes (*vihāra*) may still encounter adverse conditions and retreat from their resolve.

Thus we know that practitioners of the Three Vehicles, though traversing *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, find their meritorious practices remain unaccomplished, whereas through the gate of Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti*), one attains the stage of non-retrogression in the mere twinkling of an eye. This is...
Those born in the Pure Land advance and do not regress; they are certain to attain Buddhahood. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states:
"All those born in the land of Ultimate Bliss are *avaivartika*. *Avaivartika* refers to the stage of non-retrogression. Alas!
For those with shallow faith at the initial stage, it is difficult to progress through practice without the power of others (*tariki*). Yet, the Vow of our Buddha is profound; it is simply—

All who have the karmic affinity are fully embraced. O virtuous ones, from the time the Buddhas and Patriarchs above established the teachings, they have revealed the Dharma-gate of Buddha-recitation;
how much more so for the practitioners of Chan today who do not believe in rebirth in the Pure Land? For those who cultivate the Pure Land, there is no hindrance to the practice of Chan.
Why, then, do those who practice Chan disparage the Pure Land and fail to cultivate it? Someone may ask: "As for Amitābha..."
"Does Amitābha Buddha have a stage of practice (yin-di)?* Zongben replied: 'The stage of practice of Amitābha Buddha is recorded extensively in the Tripitaka teachings.

When I was practicing for Buddhahood, my preaching of sutras and performance of the Way were ten times greater than those of all other Buddhas. If I had not attained this vow... *(Note: "Yin-di" refers to the causal ground or preparatory stage prior to attaining Buddhahood.)
"I shall never become a Buddha unless I can fulfill this vow: that those who invoke my name shall certainly be born in my land.

Because his vows are vast and his conditions are powerful, he moves the hearts of all people. Furthermore, one does not see [this] in the verses of praise for the Buddha by the Bodhisattva Mahāmaitrī, which state:
"Among the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time, Amitābha is foremost. This is praised not only by bodhisattvas, but by [all beings].
Even the Buddhas of the ten directions praise this. Question: There are immeasurable people in the worlds of the ten directions who practice mindfulness of the Buddha;
can [the Buddha] know all of them at all times and lead them all across? Answer:

The sun and moon belong to a single small world-system (*sāhasra-cūḍika-lokadhātu*), yet their radiance can still universally illuminate all myriad things. How much more so the radiance of a Buddha! As the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "That Buddha..."
For what reason is he named Amitābha? Śāriputra, the light of that Buddha is immeasurable; it illuminates the lands of the ten directions without obstruction.
For this reason, he is named Amitābha. You should know that the light of that Buddha is vast and beyond compare.

Even the Arhats of the Hīnayāna possess the three knowledges and six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), manifesting transformations according to the various types of beings; how much more so, then, the wondrous efficacy of the Buddha’s supernormal powers?

Why is this? If one constantly pays homage to the Buddha with the body, the Buddha sees them because of the supernormal power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*). If one constantly recollects the Buddha with the mouth...
The Buddha hears this through his divine ear faculty (*divya-śrotra-abhijñā*). His mind constantly remembers them through his knowledge of others' minds (*para-citta-jñāna-abhijñā*).
O virtuous ones, you need only practice with sincere devotion yourself; there is no need to doubt that the Buddha lacks the power to guide and receive you.
He asked again: "Since there are such merits as these, why must one raise the thought [of the Buddha] with continuous recitation?
For example, when calling someone by their name, one need only do so once, twice, or thrice. He replied: "Did I not say before that by invoking my name, one will certainly be born in my land?
This is due to my vow. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: 'A single recitation of the name of Amitābha Buddha extinguishes eight hundred million kalpas of karmic obstacles.'"

This applies even to the heavy sins of birth and death throughout kalpas, let alone when the chanting continues without interruption. The *Amitābha Sūtra* states: "By virtue of reciting the name, all transgressions are extinguished.

The *Śrī-Ārya-Avalokiteśvara-Bodhisattva-Samantamukha-parivarta* (The Universal Gate of Avalokiteśvara) states: "If one recollects the Buddha and contemplates the Buddha, one will certainly see the Buddha.

From the highest level of single-mindedness without distraction and the exclusive upholding of the name, down to the successful accomplishment of ten recitations, one will be reborn in the Pure Land; this is precisely what is meant.
The Three Great Sages Manifest Themselves to Encourage Practice of the Pure Land:
Shi Huiji of Wangji Temple in Luoyang during the Tang Dynasty. Having received the full precepts during the reign of Emperor Zhongzong, he encountered the Tripitaka Master Yijing.

He personally traveled to India (Zhugan), whereupon he conceived a deep admiration for its ways. Vowing to journey to the Western Regions, he first embarked on a ship to cross the sea; after three years, he reached India.
There, he sought out Sanskrit manuscripts and visited virtuous teachers, traveling alone and solitary through the snow-capped mountains and the lands of the Hu.
There was nowhere he did not reach. Having endured much suffering, he grew deeply weary of Jambudvīpa and sighed, saying: "In which country or in which direction is there joy without suffering?
What dharma or what practice can lead one to see the Buddha swiftly? He questioned the Tripitaka masters throughout India, all of whom praised the Pure Land;
this accorded with the Golden Mouth [of the Buddha]. As for its swiftness, it is the path for a single lifetime; having exhausted this retributive body, one will surely [attain liberation].

"I shall attain rebirth there. Having heard this, he received it with reverence upon his head. Gradually traveling northeast toward the royal city of Gandhāra in North India, he came to a great mountain where there was a statue of Avalokiteśvara.
For seven days, he prostrated himself in prayer, vowing to end his life through fasting.
On the night of the seventh day, Avalokiteśvara appeared in the air in a purple-golden form, extending his right [hand].
He stroked the crown of the Sun’s head and said, "If you wish to transmit the Dharma for the benefit of yourself and others, there is only the Land of Amitābha Buddha in the West;
you must exhort people to practice mindfulness of the Buddha, recite the sutras, and vow to be reborn there.

Once you have reached that land, you will see the Buddha and me, and you shall naturally understand that the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land surpasses all other practices. Having spoken, he suddenly vanished. The Sun, exhausted from his fast, heard this—
This was his final journey. Upon ascending the mountain passes and returning to the east, he calculated that he had traveled through more than seventy countries over a total of eighteen years.
In the seventh year of the Kaiyuan era, he finally arrived in Chang’an, where he presented to the Emperor the true image of the Buddha, Sanskrit manuscripts, and other items.
He was granted the title "Master Tripitaka Dharma Master Cimin."
Furthermore, in the second year of the Dali era of the Tang dynasty, Master Fazhao resided at Yunfeng Temple in Hengzhou.

He practiced diligently without slackening, making the exhortation of others to practice Buddha-recitation his primary concern. One day, within his alms bowl during the morning gruel in the Sangha hall, the magnificent scenery of Mount Wutai appeared twice.
Within that magnificent scenery, there was further a temple; in the temple was a golden plaque inscribed with the words: "The Bamboo Grove of the Great Sage."
At that monastery, he conceived a heart of longing and yearning, desiring to pay homage at Mount Wutai. On the thirteenth day of the eighth month of the fourth year, he set out.
On the fifth day of the fourth month of the fifth year, he arrived at Wutaixian. From afar, he beheld the Buddha-light: several streaks of white light to the south of the temple.
On the sixth day, he reached Foguang Temple. That night, during the fourth watch, he saw a single beam of light descending from the northern mountain.
Shexiao (Sheshao) entered the hall in haste and asked the assembly, "What auspicious sign is this? A monk replied, "This is the inconceivable light of the Great Sage.
Upon hearing that Changjue had a karmic connection with it, Sheshao immediately prepared his formal robes and followed the light to the temple.
Fifty *li* to the northeast of the monastery, there is indeed a mountain. At the foot of the mountain is a ravine, and at the north of the ravine is a stone gate.

There, two youths dressed in green, appearing to be eight or nine years of age and possessing handsome features, were seen standing at the entrance of the gate. One was named Sudhana and the other Nanda.
Upon seeing them, [the pilgrim] rejoiced; they exchanged greetings and performed salutations, then led him through the gate and proceeded northward.
After traveling five or six *li*, he saw a golden gate tower; upon reaching it, he found it was a monastery.
Before the monastery was a golden plaque inscribed with the words "Great Sage Zhulin Monastery," exactly as he had seen it within the bowl.

It was approximately twenty *li* in circumference and contained one hundred and twenty courtyards, each with a jeweled pagoda that adorned the grounds. Everything there was made of pure gold, including flowing channels and flowering trees.
It filled the interior and shone into the temple, reaching the lecture hall.
There he saw Mañjuśrī to the west and Samantabhadra to the east, each seated upon a lion throne, the sound of their preaching clearly audible.

To the left and right of Mañjuśrī were more than ten thousand bodhisattvas, and Samantabhadra was likewise surrounded by countless bodhisattvas. The light reached the presence of the two bodhisattvas, whereupon [he] prostrated and questioned them.
He said, "Ordinary beings of the final age are far removed from the Sages; their spiritual knowledge has grown inferior and their defilements and obstructions are even deeper.
The Buddha-dharma is vast and profound, and we do not yet know how to practice it. Among all the dharma-gates, which is the most swift and essential?
Mañjuśrī replied, "That you now recollect the Buddha is precisely the right time. Among all gates of practice, none surpasses the recollection of the Buddha. Why is this? Because in the past..."
In a past kalpa, because he recollected the Buddha, he attained the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Therefore, all the dharmas of the Buddhas—the profound *prajñāpāramitā* and meditative concentrations, up to and including the Buddhas themselves—all arise from the recollection of the Buddha.
Thus, know that the recollection of the Buddha is the king of all dharmas. You should constantly recollect the Unsurpassed Dharma King without ceasing. [This will] illuminate...
He asked again, "How should one practice mindfulness? Mañjuśrī replied, "To the west of this world, there is Amitābha Buddha.
The power of that Buddha’s vows is inconceivable; you should maintain mindfulness of him without interruption. After the end of your life, you will certainly be reborn there and never fall back.
Having said these words, the two great sages each extended their golden hands and stroked the crown of his head.
He bestowed a prediction of future enlightenment upon him. Having heard this, Zhao was filled with joy and leaped for gladness; he paid his respects in thanks and withdrew.
These two accounts above are recorded in the *Song Gaoseng Zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song), both found within the Fu volume of the Tripitaka.

The *Sūtra on the Great Amitāyus* (Wuliangshou jing), which represents the ultimate aim of the sūtras and śāstras, states: The Buddha told Maitreya, "In this world, there are seventy-two billion non-retrogressive bodhisattvas who will be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss.
The number of bodhisattvas of minor practice is beyond calculation. Furthermore, [it continues:]

Not only is it so in our own land, but throughout the worlds of the ten directions, immeasurable multitudes of great bodhisattvas all mindfully recite the name of Amitābha Buddha and vow to dwell in the land of Amitābha Buddha.

The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* states: "If there be good sons or good daughters who hear the name of Amitābha Buddha and hold it fast, by virtue of reciting that name, all their transgressions shall be extinguished.
When such a person approaches the end of life, they shall immediately attain rebirth in the Land of Ultimate Bliss of Amitābha Buddha.
Śākyamuni Buddha said: "You all should believe and accept my words."
And as spoken by all the Buddhas: if there are sentient beings who hear this teaching, they should make a vow to be born in that land.
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Sixteen Contemplations Sutra) says: "If good men or good women merely hear the names of the Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas..."
This alone is sufficient to eliminate the sins of birth and death accumulated over immeasurable kalpas; how much more so for one who, with every thought, recites "Namo Amitābha Buddha" even once!
You should know that such a person is a *puṇḍarīka* lotus among men, and that Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and Mahāsthāmaprāpta Bodhisattva will be their supreme friends.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Buddha is the unsurpassed Dharma King, and the great Bodhisattvas serve as his ministers of the Dharma.

Among all those whom the ministers revere, there is only the Buddha, the Dharma King. There was once a Bodhisattva who reflected that in the past he had slandered the *Prajñāpāramitā*, whereby he fell into the evil realms and underwent immeasurable suffering.
Furthermore, although he practiced other paths for immeasurable kalpas thereafter, he was unable [to attain liberation]."
I have emerged from the ocean of suffering. Later, I encountered a spiritual friend who taught me to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha;
immediately, my karmic obstacles were extinguished, and I was reborn in the Pure Land. I should now offer my prostrations of gratitude to Amitābha Buddha. Why is this?
Because my parents, relatives, friends, human kings, and celestial deities were unable to deliver me and enable my escape from the ocean of suffering; only Amitābha Buddha’s vow [could do so].

Through this empowerment, one is able to emerge from the ocean of suffering. As a verse says: "If a person aspires to become a Buddha and keeps Amitābha in mind, he shall immediately attain the manifestation of that body;
therefore, I take refuge and pay homage. Furthermore, it is said: In the time of the Buddha, an old man sought to leave the household life, but Śāriputra did not permit it.
The Buddha observed this man and saw that in a past kalpa, while gathering *dhava* wood, he had been pursued by a tiger and climbed a tree.
Losing his voice, he called out, "Namo Buddha. Possessing this slight merit, he encountered the Buddha and attained deliverance, realizing the fruit of Arhatship. Alas!
If merely uttering His name once can lead to liberation, how much more so for those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha throughout their entire lives?

The *Lianzong baojian* states: "Amitābha is truly the compassionate father of all sentient beings; therefore, as soon as one invokes his precious name, one has already cast the seed into the lotus womb.
Once bodhicitta is aroused, one’s name is immediately inscribed upon the golden ground. To have shallow faith and fail to uphold [the practice] is a great folly and a grave error.
It is lamentable that we live in this final age, where many follow the current of deluded views and disparage pure karma as being merely provisional."
To deride the practice of reciting and upholding [the sutras] as a coarse activity—is this not to be mired in the burning house, willingly accepting eternal sinking and delusion?
The *Essential Gate to the Contemplation of the Pure Land Realm* states: "As for the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, it is the means by which sentient beings of the末世 (final age) are born..."
It is the primary gateway to death and the vessel for crossing the ocean of suffering. Once born there, one never regresses.
With a golden body, one travels through the air with sovereign ease, free from the afflictions of tigers, wolves, lions, mosquitoes, gadflies, fleas, and lice;
and untormented by thunder, lightning, wind, rain, cold, heat, hunger, or thirst. One is born by transformation within a lotus flower, with an immeasurable lifespan.
Since it is free from the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death, it is called the World of Ultimate Bliss.
Therefore, I, Śākyamuni Tathāgata, wishing to enable the beings in this land who are lost in delusion to escape all suffering, have opened the gate of subduing;

and Amitābha, the Compassionate Father, has shown the path of gathering and sustaining. For this reason, with earnest and repeated care, he has specifically praised the Pure Land and universally exhorted others to be reborn there.
It is precisely because of this. The *Anleji* (Collection on Peace and Bliss) states: "To be able to mindfully recite the name of Amitābha Buddha is to sever all karmic obstructions.
It is like a person who uses a lion’s sinew as a lute string; when its sound is played once, all other strings are severed.
It is also like a person who takes the milk of cows, sheep, donkeys, and horses and places it in a single vessel; if one then brings a lion..."
If a single drop of milk is poured into it, all the other milk will be transformed entirely into water. Likewise, if a person can maintain mindfulness of Amitābha Buddha within the mind of Bodhi,
all evil Māras and obstacles will naturally vanish, and they shall attain birth in the Pure Land.
The *Mahāyāna Moon-Treasury Sūtra* states: "In the age of the Final Dharma, though billions upon billions of sentient beings may give rise to the path of practice, not a single one attains it.
This is because in this world of the five turbidities, mixed studies lead to failure in accomplishment. Only the single gate of the Pure Land provides a passable path of entry.
One should know that while self-effort is difficult to perfect, reliance on other-power is easily achieved—just as a lowly man may ascend by attaching himself to a universal monarch."
As for the power [of this practice]: to soar and travel through the four heavens by means of ordinary substance is the merit of borrowed elixirs;

yet to ascend to the Three Isles is truly a path easy to traverse, wherein one swiftly attains resonance with the truth. Your compassionate instructions are earnest and repeated; they must be engraved upon these famished bones.
The *Ratnarāja-śāstra* states: "One who bathes in the great ocean has already utilized the waters of the hundred rivers; one who recites the Buddha’s name will necessarily achieve samādhi.
It is just as when a clear pearl is cast into turbid water—the turbid water cannot fail to become clear;
when mindfulness of the Buddha is applied to a distracted mind—the distracted mind cannot fail to become the Buddha."
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If a person recollects the Buddha with a distracted mind, they shall still be freed from suffering, and their merit will be inexhaustible;
how much more so for those who recollect the Buddha with a concentrated mind! From the highest level of 'one-pointedness without distraction' down to the successful completion of ten recitations."

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "It would be better to undergo the sufferings of hell than to receive the names of the Buddhas; it is not better to enjoy immeasurable bliss while failing to hear the names of the Buddhas.
The "Chapter on the Difficulty of Hearing the True Dharma" states: "The Buddha taught that the people of this world who are able to hear the name of Amitābha Buddha [attain great merit]."
If one feels joy through a compassionate heart, with a pure mind such that the hair on the body stands on end and tears immediately flow forth,
this person has constantly practiced the Buddha-way over many lifetimes and is no ordinary person. If you do not believe the Buddha’s words, do not believe in the practice of nianfo,

and do not believe that those reborn [in the Pure Land] all come from the evil realms because their remaining karmic retributions have not yet been exhausted— then it is because of your ignorance and lack of understanding that I speak thus for your sake.
He preached this Great Dharma, causing them to behold Amitābha Buddha and his land.
The *Hukou jing* (Sutra on Guarding the Mouth) states that there was a hungry ghost of hideous appearance, from whose body issued fierce flames and from whose mouth issued maggots.
With pus and blood, all manner of decay, and a stench so foul it permeates afar, he wails aloud and runs hither and thither.
At that time, a perfected Arhat asked him, "What sins did you commit in your past life that you now undergo such suffering? The hungry ghost replied, "In my former times..."
In a previous life as a śramaṇa, he uttered an evil word that obstructed another’s faith and goodness; thus he now encounters this suffering.

When the Venerable One returns to Jambudvīpa, he shall admonish the bhikṣus: whenever you see anyone performing even the slightest act of virtue, you should only respond with joy and provide assistance.
"Do not let it be ruined or thwarted and fail to be accomplished. Since I fell among the evil classes, I have suffered for many thousands of millions of kalpas.
Even if I were to escape and regain the form of a ghost, I would enter hell once again. When the hungry ghost had finished speaking these words, he wailed and threw himself to the ground.
It is like a great mountain collapsing; hearing such a teaching truly makes one’s heart tremble with cold fear.
If a ghost suffers through many kalpas for uttering a single evil word, how can one possibly obstruct others from bowing to the Buddha and reciting His name?
The *Vajra Ritual Manual* states: "Even wild foxes listen to Baizhang’s Dharma; even snails protect the *Diamond Sūtra*.
Ten thousand swimming fish, upon hearing the Buddha’s name, were transformed into celestial sons; five hundred bats, hearing the sound of the Dharma, all became sages and worthies.

A python heard the repentance ritual and was reborn in heaven; a dragon heard the Dharma and awakened to the Way. If those creatures were still able to comprehend and realize it, how much more so [should humans]?"
Can one not turn the mind to recite the Buddha’s name?
The *Lianzong baojian* states: "In the past, our Dharma-treasury [Dharmākara] Bodhisattva made great vows, opening the profound path to Ultimate Bliss;
thus the World-Honored Buddha pointed toward the West, revealing the wondrous realm for Vaidehī. This is praised in unison by the broad and long tongue that covers the world."

While all other sutras have come to an end, this one alone remains. This is because the Bodhisattva’s joy and renunciation in benefiting sentient beings increased, and the magnitude of his compassionate response and transformation became vast.
The teachings are divided into nine grades, thereby opening a separate door of expedient means. Contemplating the clarity of the One Mind is truly the direct path for returning to the source.
When the holy nun encountered this, it was like a long-traveling guest returning to her hometown; thus, the Way of resonance and response intersected.
It is like an infant casting itself into the arms of a compassionate mother; how much more so when one is embraced by the compassionate light! The power of the Buddha is inconceivable.

It is like riding a boat downstream, requiring no personal exertion; it is like pushing a door and falling into a mortar—how could there be anything else? Where there is a vow, there is surely a welcome; where there is no capacity for the teaching, none is excluded.
Even the śuka and kalaviṅka birds still sing forth the sounds of the Dharma; even the wriggling and crawling insects all receive the grace of transformation and edification.

O Compassionate One! The realm of the sages is not false, and the words of the Buddha are not deceptive. Why, then, do you submit your will with such resignation, welcoming calamity and delighting in disaster?
You revile the land of purity while craving this world of afflictions; like moths scorched by flame or silkworms consumed by their own cocoons, you dwell amidst lingering misfortune.
Like caged birds or fish in a cauldron, you instead claim to find happiness—all because the power of your virtue is slight while the power of karma prevails, and the root of faith is meager.
The roots of transgression are many. Thus, the three realms are vast and desolate, and the four modes of birth are turbulent and restless.
All strive for life with weary persistence; all pursue their karma with endless wandering. Were it not for the good fortune of past lives, how could one encounter such a cause?
The drum is beaten to open the gates of the prison—this is the time to emerge swiftly. A boat is encountered to rescue those drowning in the depths—how can one hesitate? Universally...

The bliss of the West—who can awaken to it? Its people and its land are entirely sublime; there is no cold or heat, nor are there the three evil realms. Within the womb of the lotus flower...
They emerge, hearing the sound of the Dharma and celestial music; the lapis lazuli ground is so brilliant it excludes even the finest dust.
Towers and pavilions are formed of gold, silver, jewels, and pearls; transformed robes and transformed food naturally flourish. Their lifespan is immeasurable and difficult to calculate.

"Believe me, the Tathāgata has said: the Buddha never speaks words that are not true.
Just as fire fanned by the wind requires no further effort to grow, if one fortunately possesses the mind of *buddhānusmṛti* (mindfulness of the Buddha), one may vow to transcend the triple world.
Someone asked Chan Master Yongming Shou: "If merely seeing one's nature and awakening to the Way allows one to transcend birth and death, why is it necessary to [practice...]"
"Those who contemplate that Buddha and seek rebirth in another land," he asked, "should answer thus: A true practitioner of cultivation ought to examine themselves.

As one who drinks water knows for themselves whether it is cold or warm, you virtuous ones, should observe your own conduct and understanding: Have you truly attained the vision of nature and awakened to the Way?

Can one match the Great Master Zhizhe of Tiantai regarding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*, being proficient in both doctrine and practice while cultivating both conduct and understanding?
