Since ancient times, the sages have received the Buddha’s mandate; they are certainly not mistaken regarding the world. The *Fourfold Selection* says:
"Those who have Chan but no Pure Land—nine out of ten go astray. When the realm of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) manifests, they are instantly carried away by it.

Those who have no Chan but have the Pure Land—of ten thousand who practice, ten thousand go. Once you have seen Amitābha, why worry about whether you have attained enlightenment? Those who have both Chan and the Pure Land..."
"Earth! You are like a horned tiger. In this life you act as a teacher to men; in future lives you shall become a Buddha or a Patriarch.
No Chan, no Pure Land—only the iron bed and the copper pillar. For ten thousand kalpas and a thousand lifetimes, there will be no one to rely upon.

Since you do not understand the principles of the Buddha and yet have no desire for rebirth in the Pure Land, you will sink into samsara for eternal kalpas; by what means can you escape? O virtuous ones, if you wish to transcend birth..."
One will swiftly realize Bodhi after death. Among these four types [of practice], choose and cultivate the wholesome conduct.
Chan Master Ze of Changlu exhorted people, saying: "The Sutra states that the sentient beings of that land have no manifold sufferings and experience only various joys;
therefore, it is named 'Ultimate Bliss' (Sukhāvatī). Now, if we contrast this with the Sahā world: here, one possesses a physical body of flesh and blood."
All that has birth is suffering; they, however, are born by transformation from lotus flowers and thus lack the suffering of birth.

Here, the seasons shift in succession and decay daily encroaches; there, cold and heat do not change, and thus there is no suffering of aging. Here, the four great elements are difficult to harmonize.

In this world, many illnesses and afflictions arise; there, the transformed body is fragrant and pure, free from the suffering of disease. In this world, those who reach seventy are rare, and impermanence is swift;
there, the lifespan is immeasurable, free from the suffering of death. In this world, there is attachment to kinsmen and loved ones.
Where there is craving, one must inevitably part from those objects; there are no parents, wives, or children, and thus there is no suffering of being separated from what one loves.
Here, however, there are enemies and adversaries; where there are enemies, they must inevitably meet, yet there is no suffering of meeting with what one hates.
Here, there is the hardship of poverty, hunger, and cold, with insatiable greed for more; there, clothing, food, and precious treasures are provided for use as soon as they appear. Here, perhaps—
This [body] is a loathsome physical frame with many deficient and leaking faculties; that [body] possesses dignified features and its form radiates light.
This one revolves through birth and death; that one has eternally realized the non-arising of phenomena. This place is filled with hills, mounds, pits, and ravines, where thorns form forests.

Whereas this place is filled with earth, stones, and mountains, and abounds in filth and impurity, that realm has the ground of pure gold, with jewel-trees reaching to the heavens, towers soaring with the seven treasures, and flowers blooming in four colors.
Here, the twin śāla trees have already perished and the Dragon Flower [Buddha] has not yet appeared;

there, Amitābha Buddha currently dwells and preaches the Dharma. Here, Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta can only look up to their illustrious names; there, they [are present] together with those two...
In this [realm], superior persons act as one's true spiritual friends; whereas there, the various māras and heterodox teachers disturb and confuse right practice.
In this [realm], the Buddha’s transformation unifies all under his rule, while māras and heretics are utterly restrained; whereas there, seductive forms and lascivious charms delude practitioners.
In this [realm], the physical retribution is pure and there are truly no women; whereas there, evil beasts and malevolent spirits spread perverse sounds together. In this [realm], the water birds...

In the groves of trees, the wondrous Dharma is proclaimed everywhere. When comparing these two lands, their environments and conditions differ; yet the excellence of the Land of Bliss is beyond measure.

Therefore, among the definitive Mahāyāna teachings, there is none that does not point toward the Pure Land. Sages of the past and present, both for themselves and others, have all vowed to be reborn there.
Alas! If people lack far-sighted concern, they will surely face immediate distress. Once this human body is lost, ten thousand...

As the kalpa calamities are about to recur, I therefore lead the great assembly of the ocean; each shall mindfully recite the name of Amitābha Buddha and dedicate their roots of goodness with a shared aspiration to be born in that land.
Just as when one boards a boat and follows the current, if one also applies oars and paddles, a journey of a hundred thousand leagues will reach its destination effortlessly.
In the winter of the fourth year of the Yuanyou era, Zongze dreamed one night of a man wearing a black cap and white robes, appearing to be about thirty years of age.
His appearance was refined and beautiful, and his demeanor was noble and elegant. He bowed to Zongze and said, "I wish to enter your Amitābha assembly;
please record my name. Zongze then took up the *Record of the Lotus Supreme Assembly* and, holding his pen, asked, "Sir—"
"What is your name? he asked. "It is Puhui (Universal Wisdom)," the man replied. After Zongze had finished writing, the layman said again, "My elder brother also told me your name.
Zongze asked, "What is your elder brother's name? "It is Puxian (Universal Virtue)," he replied. Having spoken, the man suddenly vanished.
Upon waking, Zongze inquired of the senior monks, all of whom said, "In the 'Chapter on Leaving the World' of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, there are two great Bodhisattvas by these names."
Zongze believed that when a son of the Buddha performs the Buddha’s work and assists the Buddha in propagating his transformation, there must be the subtle assistance of worthy sages.
Thus, how could those who participate in this assembly have anything other than profound karmic conditions?

The layman Wang of Longshu exhorted people, saying: "The *Great Amitābha Sūtra* states that there are immeasurable bodhisattvas in the ten directions who are reborn in the land of Amitābha Buddha. If even those bodhisattvas desire to be reborn there, what am I?
I shall briefly cite several instances as proof. Qingcaotang was the reincarnation of the late Duke Zeng; the Elder Zhe was the reincarnation of [the monk] Duōyōu."
It is suffering. The old woman’s final incarnation was one who was addicted to wealth and status; the nun of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*’s final incarnation became a court courtesan.

Both failed to believe in the Western Paradise and thus transmigrated through the cycle of rebirth, undergoing suffering. Someone asked: "While it is indeed difficult to realize one's nature through Zen meditation, how does learning the arts of the immortals (*xian*) compare?"

Answer: To wish to study the arts of the immortals (*ṛṣi*) without cultivating the Pure Land is like discarding a beautiful jade before one’s eyes to seek a *wǔfū* stone that cannot necessarily be obtained;

is this not delusion? According to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, there are ten kinds of immortals, all of whom live for ten million years; yet when their lifespan is exhausted, they re-enter the cycle of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
Among those in the world who study the arts of the immortals, not even one in ten thousand succeeds; and even if they should succeed, [they still fall back].
Furthermore, one cannot avoid the cycle of *saṃsāra*, for one is attached to form and spirit and is unable to relinquish them.

Moreover, form and spirit are merely delusive thoughts manifested within the true nature. Thus, Hanshan’s poem says: "Even if you were to become an immortal, you would be no different from a ghost guarding a corpse.
This is not like the Buddhist state where one is at ease amidst birth and death, free from all constraints. Recently, from...

Over several hundred years, those who attained the state of an immortal were only Zhongli Quan and Lü Dongbin. Have you not heard how Lü Dongbin flew his sword to slay the Yellow Dragon, only to be subdued by that very dragon?
It was only upon meeting the Chan Master Huanglong that he finally awakened to his true nature and perfected the Way.
He then spoke a verse, saying: "I have cast away my gourd vessel and smashed my zither; Now I no longer cherish the gold within the eternal [world].
Since first meeting Huanglong, I have finally realized that all my previous efforts were misplaced. Furthermore, have you not heard of Dharma Master Tanluan of the Later Wei?
Initially, he obtained ten scrolls of the *Cinnabar Scripture* from Tao Hongjing. Delighted, Tanluan considered himself to have attained the divine.
"The Immortal can certainly be attained. Later, he encountered the monk Bodhiruci, who asked him, "In the Way of the Buddha, is there eternal life?
Can one ward off old age and achieve immortality? Bodhiruci replied, "Eternal life and immortality are precisely my Buddhist Way.

He then gave him the *Sūtra on the Sixteen Contemplations*, saying, "You should recite this; then you will no longer be reborn within the three realms, nor will you again wander through the six destinies."
Regarding the waxing and waning, the arising and ceasing, fortune and misfortune, or success and failure—none of these can reach it.
As for its longevity, there are the *kalpa-stones* and the grains of the Ganges River. While the number of such sands and stones is finite, the measure of this lifespan is infinite;

this is the "long life" of our Golden Immortal (the Buddha). Luán believed this deeply and consequently burned the scriptures of the immortals to devote himself exclusively to the practice of the *Amitābha Sūtra*. Even in the cold...
Even amidst the changes of summer and the onset of illness, he did not slacken in his resolve. King Wei, moved by his lofty aspirations, bestowed upon him the title "Divine Crane.
One day, he told his disciples: "The various sufferings of the hells must not be taken lightly; one must fear them. As for the pure karma of the nine grades,"
One must not fail to practice. Consequently, he had his disciples chant the name of Amitābha Buddha in a loud voice.
Sengluan faced west, closed his eyes, prostrated himself, and passed away. At that time, both monks and laypeople alike heard the sound of pipes, strings, and flutes coming from the west.
Judging by this, the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land is the most direct path; how much more so for those who have attained the status of immortals?
Thus, [the former] keep [their teachings] secret and do not transmit them, claiming that to leak celestial mechanisms (*tianji*) constitutes a transgression.
As for the gates of the Buddha-dharma, they fear only that its transmission may not be widespread; they desire nothing less than to deliver every single sentient being before they cease.
It is clear that such vast compassion is not comparable to that of the immortals (*shenxian*).

Prime Minister Zheng Qingzhi exhorted people, saying: "Among those who study Buddhism today, there are none who go beyond Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya. As for the ultimate, sudden, and perfect path, nothing compares to Chan;

yet unless one possesses sharp faculties and superior capacity, and is able to grasp it through spiritual intuition and intellectual understanding, one cannot avoid falling into the error of 'stolid emptiness.

For the thorough investigation of the Three Vehicles, nothing compares to the Teaching; yet unless one is able to forget the trap upon catching the fish, or see the moon by following the pointing finger, [one will fail to reach the truth]."
This avoids the malady of poring over mere dry texts. In protecting the good and warding off evil, nothing compares to the Vinaya.
Unless one’s body and mind are pure and their inner and outer states are as one, one cannot escape the suffering of self-entanglement. As for the path entered, it is Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya;

as for the ultimate destination, it is Precepts, Concentration, and Wisdom. If one were to attain Precepts, Concentration, and Wisdom without relying on Chan, Teaching, and Vinaya, who could it possibly be?
"Is this not one gate to the Pure Land?
Longshu said: "The Avataṃsaka Sūtra states: 'There are two kinds of people in the world: those who follow devas and humans, and those who are born with the same name as them.

Are these not the disciples of the two classes of evil youths? When a person raises an intention, speaks a word, or takes a step, they should constantly keep these two heavenly beings in mind;
thus, when seeing others, they will be free from shame. If one cultivates the Pure Land in this manner, they will certainly attain birth in the highest grade of the highest level.
Someone may ask: "If there are already two heavenly beings for a single person, why are there so many heavenly beings? [The Master] replied: "The moon universally manifests itself in a single..."
"Cutting water—how could it necessarily be a great deed?

There are those who sit in palanquins and those who carry them; these are the minor fruits of heaven and hell.
Extending this principle to all similar cases, what doubt could there be regarding the attainment of rebirth in the highest grade of the Pure Land through cultivation?
It is further said: "Day must be followed by night; one must prepare for the night. Heat must be followed by cold; one must prepare for the cold.

Existence must be followed by departure; one must prepare for departure. What is meant by preparation for the night? Lamps, candles, bedding, and mats. What is meant by preparation for the cold? Quilts, furs, charcoal, and firewood.
What is meant by preparation for departure? Merit, wisdom, and the Pure Land."
Furthermore, he said: "I have examined the Tripitaka thoroughly, yet I find no doctrine regarding 'depositing goods in the underworld.

I exhort the people of the world to use the funds intended for such deposits to instead invite monks to perform offerings for the Western Paradise. If one directs the mind single-mindedly toward the West, one will surely attain rebirth there.
If, instead of performing meritorious acts for the Pure Land, one performs 'deposits in the underworld,' then one's intent is fixed upon the underworld."
The Prefecture: Upon death, one must certainly enter the Netherworld (Yin-fu). It is like a person who, failing to practice the conduct of a gentleman, seeks to associate with the worthy;

yet that gentleman entrusts money to the Court of Judicial Review (Si-li-yuan), waiting for his client to be cast into prison so that the funds may be used to secure his release from punishment—is this not utterly absurd?
Formerly, Zhang Shanhe spent his entire life slaughtering oxen; at the moment of his death, he saw the earth [crack open] before him.

The signs of hell appeared; she encountered a monk who instructed her to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha. Before she had finished ten recitations, she saw the Buddha coming to welcome her, and she was reborn in the Pure Land.

By virtue of these four phrases, she also attained rebirth in the Pure Land—how much more so for one who recites the entire [sutra].
How could it be that one does not attain rebirth in the [Buddha] family? Dharma Master Tanyi was a pheasant in his previous life;

upon hearing a monk reciting the *Lotus Sūtra*, he immediately attained rebirth as a monk and realized the Way. How much more so for a person who recites the sūtras and practices mindfulness of the Buddha—how could they fail to see the Buddha?
Furthermore, there were once a parrot and two magpies who, by recollecting Amitābha Buddha, attained rebirth in the Pure Land;
how much more so should a human being, who recollects the Buddha, not be reborn there?
It is also said: "It is like a person entering a great city; they must first seek a place to settle before going out to attend to their business.
When evening falls and it becomes dark, they will have a place to lodge. 'Seeking a place to settle first' refers to the cultivation of the Pure Land."
"Arriving at twilight and darkness" refers to the arrival of one's great destiny (the end of life).

"Having a place to lodge for the night" refers to being born within a lotus flower and not falling into the evil realms. It is also like traveling far during the spring months; one must first prepare for rain.
When a sudden rain falls unexpectedly, one who has prepared their rain gear in advance will suffer no distress from being soaked or falling into disarray.
"Preparing one's rain gear in advance" refers to the cultivation of the Pure Land. "A sudden rain falling unexpectedly" refers to the moment when one’s great life-force is about to end.
"Suffering no distress from being soaked or falling into disarray" refers to not sinking into the evil realms to undergo various sufferings. Furthermore, one must first seek security.
Being in a low station does not hinder one from attending to one's own affairs; first prepare for the rain, and you will not be hindered when traveling far.
Cultivating the Pure Land does not hinder one in any worldly duties—why, then, would anyone not practice it? Even those who are sinful can cultivate it;
for example, although iron and stone are heavy, they can be crossed over by relying on a boat, whereas a needle, though light, cannot cross without relying on a boat.

It cannot be crossed. A person with grave offenses may be reborn in the Pure Land by relying on the power of the Buddha; yet even those with minor offenses cannot be reborn there without relying on the power of the Buddha.
It is like lice and nits: though they die and are reborn ten thousand times, they cannot travel a single *li*;

yet if they attach themselves to a human body, they can reach a thousand *li*. Those who rely on the power of the Buddha to be reborn in the Pure Land are just like this. It is through the strength [of the Buddha].
At such a time, if one has not prepared beforehand, what can be done once the eyes are closed?

It is universally known and no one dares deny that day must inevitably be followed by night, and cold must inevitably be followed by heat. Yet, when it comes to saying that birth must inevitably be followed by death, people avoid it and refuse to speak of it;
how utterly obscured they are! O virtuous ones, it is truly a great pity if you do not practice now.
Furthermore, it is said: "When a person is alive, there are all manner of affairs that do not fail to weigh upon their heart. Once the great limit [of life] arrives, they are all cast away.
Even this body of mine is but a discarded thing; how much more so that which lies outside the body? Reflecting on these words, one is suddenly enlightened.
It is like a single dream. An ancient said: "When impermanence arrives one day, only then will one know that one was a person within a dream.
Of all things, nothing can be taken away; only karma follows one. Here, "karma" refers to both wholesome and unwholesome karma—all of these are what one carries with oneself.
How could one not take the Pure Land as one’s primary practice? There was the Elder Liaoming, who, when preaching for the assembly, pointed to his own body and said:
"This is a dead thing; that which moves within it is the living thing. Do not make your livelihood upon the dead thing;
you should make your livelihood upon the living thing. I deeply cherish these words. Whenever I am greedy...
To offer various external objects to one's body is merely to make a living off of things that are destined for death.
Zhiguizi asked Master Shandao: "I have received your instructions on the method of *nienfo*, yet I fear that at the moment of death my consciousness will be distracted;

furthermore, I worry that others may disturb my right mindfulness and cause me to lose it. Master Jingyin replied: [The text continues with the Master's response regarding the importance of maintaining mindfulness and the role of companions.]
Excellent is this question. Generally, when the lives of all people come to an end, one must not fear death. One should constantly reflect that this body is full of suffering;
if one can cast it off and be reborn in a Pure Land to experience immeasurable bliss, that is truly a matter to one's heart's content—like casting off worn-out clothes to obtain precious garments.
Would anyone ever feel attachment toward those worn-out clothes? It is simply that when one encounters illness...

At that time, he immediately contemplated impermanence and waited for death with single-minded focus. He instructed his family members, as well as those who came to visit or inquire after him regarding his illness:
"Whenever anyone comes before me, you must not engage in idle or trivial conversation about worldly matters.
Nor should you offer comforting words or pray for my peace and well-being; these are all empty flowers of no benefit. If the illness becomes grave and I am approaching the end, even my relatives..."

One must not shed tears or wail, nor lament with grief that disturbs the mind and spirit. One should instead recite the Buddha’s name with a single voice to assist them in attaining rebirth in the Pure Land.
It is not too late to weep in sorrow after a long time has passed once their breath has ceased. If one understands that death is a departure, how could one not refrain from weeping?
This would be especially profound in its realization of principle; moreover, in rebirth in the Pure Land, one abandons suffering to obtain bliss.
One must be careful not to weep or wail, for this causes the mind of the deceased to become distracted.

I have also frequently observed people of the world who, in their daily lives, recite the Buddha’s name, offer praises, and make vows to seek rebirth in the Western Paradise; yet, when illness strikes, they again fear death and say nothing more of the matter of rebirth.
Only when their breath has ceased and their life-force is exhausted, as their consciousness departs for the realm of darkness, do they finally begin to chant the ten recitations.
The bell. It is just like closing the gate after the thief has gone; what benefit does it serve? The matter of birth and death is of great importance;
you must exert effort yourself before it can be resolved. If there is a single moment of error, you will suffer for kalpas on end—no one can take your place. Reflect upon this, reflect upon it!

The Lord Master Jizhao’s *Ten Gates of Admonition for the Pure Land* states: "Practitioners of the Buddha-name recitation must be careful regarding the three doubts and three barriers at the time of death.
First, one may doubt: 'I have committed extremely heavy karma since birth, while my practice has been shallow for only a few days;
I fear I shall not attain rebirth. Third, one may doubt: 'I owe debts to others, or I have unfulfilled aspirations, as well as [the presence of] greed, anger, and delusion.'"
It has not yet ceased; I fear I shall not be reborn there. Third, I harbor doubt that although I am mindful of Amitābha, the Buddha may not come to welcome and guide me at the moment of death.
Because of these three doubts, they become obstacles that cause one to lose right mindfulness and fail to attain rebirth in the Pure Land.
Therefore, those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha must earnestly and faithfully believe the clear intent of the Buddhist sutras and harbor no doubts. Regarding the three gates:

although ordinary beings may possess faith and practice mindfulness of the Buddha, because their karmic obstructions from past lives are heavy, they are destined to fall into hell; thus, at the time of death, they cannot escape the suffering of illness.
If, through the suffering of illness, they come to know repentance and awakening in both body and mind, they will certainly be reborn in the Pure Land. This is simply because...
Ignorant people do not understand this matter; instead, they say, "I am now reciting the Buddha's name, yet I still suffer from illness.
Thus, they slander Amitābha. Because of this single thought of malice, they go straight to hell. This is the first barrier.

Second, although one may observe the precepts and recite the Buddha's name, because one habitually speaks of the Pure Land while the mind and intentions still cling to this Sahā world, [one will fail].

When facing the end of life and encountering illness, one fears death and clings to life; one believes the words of children and invokes spirits and ghosts; one burns money and transforms paper, and slaughters living beings.
Because the mind is thus perverted, one lacks the protection of the Buddhas and wanders and falls into the three miserable realms—this is the second barrier.
Third, at the moment of death, one remains bound to wealth and property and is filled with attachment to one's kin; the mind is distracted and unrestrained.

Looking back at one's family, one falls into the realm of hungry ghosts; becoming either a stingy dog or a snake, one guards the household as if it were still one's own day. This is the third barrier.
The masters of old said: "Heaven and hell are arrayed on both sides; it depends on where one practices as one approaches them.

Truly, these words are true. Someone asked: "If it is as your teacher says, do the six realms and the three miserable paths truly exist, such that one wanders in saṃsāra and undergoes suffering? He replied:

If there were no six realms of rebirth, nor the three miserable paths and eight difficulties, this old monk would not have been willing to observe the precepts of fasting, abstain from wine and meat, undergo bitter Zen meditation, or diligently recite the Buddha’s name.

It is because of these sufferings of saṃsāra that I am finally willing to recite the Buddha’s name and practice, vowing to abandon this Sahā world and vow to be born in the Pure Land. I tell you this directly, O virtuous one: if you wish to see the world—
Among humans, who does not love sensual desire? Who does not enjoy wine and meat? Who does not crave fame and profit?
Who does not wish for wealth and nobility? I know that these are the very root of the suffering of saṃsāra; therefore, I neither scheme nor seek after them. The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says:
"The cause of all sufferings is rooted in craving and desire. If craving and desire are extinguished, there will be nothing upon which they can depend."
In the West, the Compassionate Father of the West is moved to sorrow by this verse of praise; He receives and guides the deluded stream of beings—return, return!
Hasten to the Lotus Throne to personally entrust your essence; Do not seek refuge in the mundane world or enter a womb.
In the Pure Land of the West lies the lotus womb; I universally exhort all sentient beings to go there.
With a single thought, the pen opens [the gate], and one sees the Buddha face-to-face; Therein, the eight difficulties and three calamities shall forever cease.
The West makes no distinction between rich and poor, Nor does it select between the wise and the foolish, the noble and the lowly.
Without distinguishing between woman or man, old or young, nor between monastic or lay, or enemy or kin—the Dharma family in the West is most closely knit;
they are all practitioners who recite the Buddha’s name.
We wish to return to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī); we shall plant the seeds for rebirth there this very moment.
The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is praised as supreme; I universally exhort all people to enter this gate.
Those with mouths need not engage in idle discourse; Simply hold the Buddha’s name to pass through morning and evening.
In the West there is a Buddha named Amitābha, Universally delivering sentient beings from the river of craving.
The Six Eight Vows open the way for the nine grades; Every person can reach it—do not let the moment slip away.
The Western Land is easy to go to, yet few know it; Cultivate the path directly and do not harbor doubts.
When the True Sutra of Six Words is fully mastered, One shall pay homage to Amitābha upon the golden lotus throne.
The Compassionate Father in the West is named Amitābha; He receives those who enter the nine grades of the lotus pond.
This shortcut Dharma door is easy to reach; Piteous are those who mostly harbor self-doubt.
The Western Land is a direct pointing, easy to practice; Who among them knows their own original nature is Amitābha?
Transmigrating through the six realms and three miserable paths of birth and death—how can one contemplate this without feeling pain and sorrow?
Haste to practice the Way of the West with urgency; the impermanence of life and death cannot be predicted.
The sunlight outside the window passes in the blink of an eye; how much time does a human being truly have?
The Westerner’s Kōan: Early Practice. In profound stillness and alert awareness, apply your intent with doubt;
reach the point where emotion is forgotten and the mind is severed. It turns out that you yourself are Amitābha.
*Zhuo’u Guiyuan Zhizhi Lun* (Zhuo’u’s Direct Pointing to the Source) says: This school is fundamentally a book by Master Yuan. It was originally intended...

I have composed this book because people are single-mindedly cultivating the Pure Land. Thus, my detailed citations and subtle proofs, intended to provide clear instruction to others, are ultimate and exhaustive.
Within them lies a truth that is both authentic and simple, which has not been revealed by other masters or their various doctrines. This is the point:

when it comes to the practice of *nianfo* (reciting the Buddha’s name), one need not first inquire who the person is; even those whose past lives have been filled with excessive evil karma [may attain rebirth].
It is erroneous to excuse oneself and refuse to practice *nien-fo* (Buddha-recitation). It is erroneous to say that at the beginning of *nien-fo*, one need not consider the time;
thus, those who use old age or the approach of death as pretexts for procrastination and refuse to practice *nien-fo* are mistaken.

It is also erroneous to say that at the beginning of *nien-fo*, one need not restrict oneself to any particular method; thus, those who establish a fixed, rigid routine [as the only way] are mistaken.
To cause a thousand people to follow the same rule and for a thousand ages to remain the same—yet to allow such a person to be hindered so as to be unable to pervade the entire earth—is a delusion.
It is only through the sincere arousal of the vow: "May I behold that Buddha Amitābha;
may I be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, forever escaping the impure suffering and afflictions of this world of five turbidities."
It is merely urgent for the person themselves; there are no such erroneous instructions intended to delude or cause others to retreat out of fear.
One can thus know that all three errors are the faults of the teacher and do not concern the student. This applies solely to the gate of the single vow.
This is of the utmost urgency. Looking broadly at the human world, who among us does not wish to be reborn in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, casting off this sea of suffering?

Who, moreover, does not wish to arrive there in a single thought-moment without expending mental effort, yet instead excuses themselves by saying, "I have no leisure to make a vow"? Therefore, know that making a vow is most urgent; once made—
The Original Vow is, moreover, the most easy matter. I know that among all sentient beings throughout the entire earth, there is not one who does not give rise to the Great Vow.
How great, then, must be the merit of our Original Teacher!
"Requesting the West Five Times;
Explaining the West. Zhuowuzi said: "The West is the Metal direction. Metal is most rigid;
it can push down and destroy all things, yet no thing can destroy it. The Buddha-nature is firm, rigid, and indestructible for this very reason, and thus it is taken as a metaphor."
Therefore, the scripture is titled *Vajra*. Furthermore, "Buddha" is a name used in the Western [region].
Now, the Dharma-body is firm and solid, signless and non-abiding; for this reason, it is indestructible. Thus it is said: "Whatever has marks is entirely false and illusory.
That which is called "false and illusory" is so because it can be destroyed. That which can be destroyed is so because it possesses [marks].
This is a characteristic. Now, where there are no characteristics, there is no dwelling; where there is no dwelling, there is no destruction.
Viewed from this perspective, the indestructible true body resides within each and every person. The Western Land of Ultimate Bliss is entirely not separate from daily life.

Yet, why is it that people are taught to exert effort, engage in *chan* (meditation), and seek the Buddha? It is not only for this reason. People are taught to practice seated meditation; people are taught...
They cultivate meditative concentration; they teach people to refine away demons; they teach people to burn their bodies; they teach people to sever their arms;

they teach people to practice the three steadfast dharmas; they teach people to relinquish body, life, and wealth; they teach people to cultivate the six perfections and myriad practices—to perform what is difficult to perform, to relinquish what is difficult to relinquish, and to endure what is difficult to endure.
Through such cultivation over vast ages and successive kalpas, one may perhaps achieve success. Is this not cultivation?
How can one who possesses the marks of a Buddha wish to realize the principle of non-arising?

How can one who accumulates causes of outflow (āsrava) hope for the fruit of eternal, outflow-free liberation? Even if one were to pass through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, one would certainly never succeed;

yet the Buddha conversely teaches people to do so. Why is this? It is because sentient beings are deluded and ignorant, and having already regarded the state of Buddhahood as something absolutely unattainable...

Furthermore, you have falsely slandered Śākyamuni, claiming that he reached his state after serving spiritual friends for immeasurable billions of kalpas and practicing with bitter hardship—something that we sentient beings cannot hope to achieve.

Now, since you consider yourself a sentient being, you already possess the mark of a sentient being (*sattva-saṃjñā*). Moreover, since you regard the Buddha as something unattainable, [you thereby deny his nature].

This is the mark of a self-cherisher (*jīvadr̥ṣṭi*). The mark of a self-cherisher is the mark of a person (*pudgaladr̥ṣṭi*); the mark of a sentient being (*sattvadr̥ṣṭi*) is the mark of a self (*ātmadr̥ṣṭi*).
These four marks are clearly present; when could one ever believe in the Buddha-work of signlessness?

Out of compassion for this, the Buddha extensively opened the gates of expedient means (*upāya*), allowing those who practice according to their own inclinations to obtain good fruits even if they do not attain Buddhahood. If there is one of great...

Regarding the power of the firm resolve of the Great Vow: after exhausting oneself through diligent toil over successive kalpas, when the day has grown dark and the road remains long, one naturally turns back and looks behind;
this is merely awakening from delusion and recognizing one's error. At this moment, if one suddenly lets go, that is true letting go;

if one suddenly attains peace and stability, that is true peace and stability. Although these kalpas of dust may have been spent in vain, were it not for this, the faculty of faith would not be established.
Profound, yet even that which is attained is not firm. For this reason, one cannot help but allow things to proceed in this manner.
However, practicing in this way will necessarily require hundreds of millions of kalpas before one finally succeeds in becoming a single Buddha. You are a son of the Buddha.
Such a person would be an unprecedented son of the Buddha in this world.

Even within the dispensation of Śākyamuni, one might gaze with eyes so worn out by longing that, throughout successive kalpas, not even a single or half a Buddha could be attained. How much more so for a human life, where moments of time are so few?
Before the age of twenty, one is deluded and ignorant of worldly affairs; after fifty, one is decayed and indolent, distracted by worldly matters.
During the intervening twenty-odd years, people merely occupy themselves with the karmic obstacles of marriage and official career.

Who among them would be willing to resolve their minds toward awakening? When it comes to speaking of this, such a person is rare indeed. Thus, the seed of the Buddha is inevitably severed. Therefore, the Buddha—
A special gate has been opened, teaching people exclusively to recite the Buddha’s name. It is said that in the Western Quarter resides Amitābha Buddha, whose power of vows is vast and great;
he will unfailingly welcome and guide all who hold his name and take refuge in the West.

According to the depth or shallowness of their power of mindfulness, they are reborn in one of the nine grades. Even those born by transformation in the lowest-of-the-low grade, though they may not...
They see the Buddha and also draw near to him, just like the officials of the two capitals and the thirteen provinces today.
Although they do not behold the Sovereign in person, they all carry out administrative orders by means of imperial seals and credentials;

everyone regards them as being appointed by the Sovereign, and those who dispatch them are revered and honored—dare anyone dare to offend them? Those who are reborn through the highest grade of transformation are like those of the present day.
These are the ministers and high officials. They receive the majestic radiance of the Most Honored One and carry out the solemn commands of the Most Honored One;
even the Great Māra kings and the Great Asura kings would retreat three paces in deference to them, let alone King Yama—how could he dare so much as open his mouth in their presence?
This is because the Buddha’s vows are vast and fundamentally true, never being in vain.
Therefore, at the moment of death, the Buddha, by the power of his vows, will come in person to receive and guide you, just as a mother seeks her child—what difficulty could there be in this?
By the power of your own faith, you will be reborn there according to your thought, just as a child remembers its mother—what danger could there be in this?
When these two intentions merge, you shall return together to the Pure Land; what doubt can there be? Moreover, with a single utterance of "Amitābha"...

It originally does not require even a hair’s breadth of effort, nor does it hinder even a single drop of worldly affairs. Holding one's staff and wearing one's sandals, one simply attends to daily duties;
it requires nothing more than a single thought of sincere faith. Who cannot do this? Who cannot recite it?

Therefore, today, from the people of the four seas and nine provinces to the nations of the four barbarians and eight tribes, a single utterance of "Amitābha" fills the three thousandfold world system.

This is why it is called the "Great Trichiliocosm. If there were anyone within it who possessed true wisdom and great resolve, they would, by virtue of mindfulness of the Buddha, immediately see the Buddha of the West for themselves; would this not indeed be a matter of supreme merit?
From this, one sees that the merit of mindfulness of the Buddha is vast. Thus, the Great Master [Zhiyi] said: "The distance from here to the West..."

There are one hundred and eight thousand [obstacles], such as the ten evils and eight perversions within the human body. If there were no such perversity and evil, [the land] would have arrived spontaneously at that time.
To speak of it as distant refers to those of inferior capacity; to speak of it as near refers to those of superior wisdom.

This is because for a person of superior wisdom, the very opening of the mouth to recite the Buddha's name is itself the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss. Since there is not a single speck of worldly defilement (*rajas*) to obstruct them, then—
This eliminates one hundred and eight thousand [obstacles]; it is not that there are separate so-called "evil thoughts" or "perverse thoughts" acting as obstructions for oneself.
Thus, teaching people to recite the Buddha’s name is nothing more than desiring that they see the Buddha. Seeing the Buddha is already simple and direct;
furthermore, rebirth [in the Pure Land] is naturally level and free of hindrance. Therefore, Chan Master Yongming Shou said:
The analogy of "ten thousand practicing and ten thousand going" states that once one is born in the Western Pure Land, one can see the Buddha, and one can also see the Buddha within oneself.
As for those who see the Buddha in the present moment, there is only a matter of speed—whether it be slow or fast.
Although they differ in speed, once the Buddha has been seen, how could there be any difference? Therefore, at this very moment, one need only have faith.

As for "the Buddha recollecting the Buddha," how could one know that this is not the result of having served spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) for billions of eons and cultivated through ascetic practices until reaching this state?
Regarding the true meaning of *nianfo* (recollection of the Buddha): what is called "recollection of the Buddha" is not the recollection of the mouth, but rather the recollection of the mind.
It is thus: that which the mind contemplates is where the imagination focuses; it is where the will inclines; it is where affection is concentrated; it is where emotion is bound;
it is the limit of thought and the certainty of planning. This can be observed in the world of men.
If there is one who takes beauty as their heart’s desire, then every thought is solely of beauty; beyond beauty, there is nothing.

A hundred other things do not enter one's mind. For those who take the management of livelihood as their primary concern, every thought is directed toward generating wealth; beyond wealth, a hundred other things do not enter their minds.
For those who take the pursuit of nobility as their primary concern, every thought is fixed on attaining status; beyond nobility, a hundred other things do not enter their minds.
This continues down through generations, with those who take the perpetuation of the human lineage as their primary concern, every thought being fixed upon it.
"Bequeath it to him. Beyond such bequeathing, there is nothing else that can satisfy the mind even a hundredfold.
Though these people spend their entire day, they have never once uttered these words aloud; yet they arrive at the goal and stand in expectation, ceaselessly day and night.

Rarely does their realization fail to correspond to their thoughts, for the mental focus with which they contemplate is firm. Even if other matters may occasionally intermingle, they ultimately remain insufficient [to distract them].
If one replaces [other thoughts] with right mindfulness, then the practitioner of Buddha-recollection can be known. For the human mind is that which is most urgent;
it is like water that must flow to the sea, fire that must blaze upward, a sharp blade that must wound, or a poisonous drug that must kill—it cannot pass by in vain.
The mindfulness of Buddha-recollection is also like this. Thus, even if one...
To recite the name of the Buddha even once is, in truth, to practice the recitation of the Buddha's name throughout the entire day.

However, if one harbors both faith and doubt—uncertain whether or not the Western Pure Land actually exists—then even if one recites the Buddha’s name as a daily ritual or adheres to a rule of a thousand recitations, it is all in vain.
For there is no principle whereby a mother who does not believe her child to be her own would fail to remember that child; yet such is the state of those who do not believe at all in the Buddha.
It is only that the grieving child does not think of their mother. If one truly concentrates the mind on the mother, then the mother will immediately appear before the child;
it is simply that the physical eye cannot see her. Why wait for another day to see her? And why wait for another day to go to her?
Furthermore, how could she be like wealth, honors, or goods, which must be accumulated before they arrive, or left to the whims of fate?
How could there be those who do not reach this destiny? Recently, I heard that three people had strange dreams.

Although these three were extremely foolish, they were nonetheless greatly terrified. This was because their dreams were so extraordinary, and upon waking, they experienced great omens; thus, they were afraid.

Having heard this, I have composed a verse on the recollection of the Buddha (nienfo) to praise them, hoping that they might perhaps be willing to turn their thoughts toward the Buddha. How regrettable!
Alas! How difficult it is for those without merit to attain liberation! They do not at all contemplate that this dream is impermanent, nor do they contemplate the Buddha.

While their very intention was to use this dream to awaken sentient beings, because their long-standing habitual thoughts remained so firm, they rushed headlong through the fires and cauldrons of hell, ultimately treating the dream as a mere social gathering.
How truly lamentable this is!
Answer: Those who inquire of the Buddha in the West are none other than these two minds. This mind is possessed by every person and inherent in every thing.
When it manifests in a way that cannot be fathomed, it is called the spirit of this mind; when it responds without being a substantial entity, it is said to transform together with all things.
Being spiritual, it cannot be confined to any particular direction; thus, it emerges into life and enters death, moving through all things without obstruction.
In a single corner, transformation leaves no trace behind. Thus, whether born or dying, changing and finally ending, all returns to the realm of illusion and falsehood.
People simply do not realize that this is the spiritual transformation of the mind; instead, they grasp at that which is spiritually transformed and claim it to be "my mind.
Consequently, they remain submerged within the cycle of birth and death, undergoing transformations throughout the turning of saṃsāra for ten thousand kalpas and a thousand aeons.

Beings undergo birth according to their shifting transformations; at times, due to an abundance of merit, they are born in the heavens, and at other times, because their enjoyment of heavenly bliss has become excessive, they descend again into the hells.
Only the sages know this field of saṃsāra and the cycle of birth and death.
It is not a place where one who possesses consciousness should dwell in peace. Therefore, at fifteen years of age, I resolved to pursue the Way.
This Way is the very ground from which spiritual transformation emerges spontaneously; it is the root of birth and death. Fundamentally, there has never been birth—how, then, could there be death?
Fundamentally, there has never been death—how, then, could there be birth? Thus it is said: "If one hears the Way in the morning, it is acceptable to die in the evening. This means it is acceptable.
By means of death, one no longer transmigrates through the six realms. Buddhists value this highly;
therefore, throughout their years and lifetimes, they spend their days discussing this principle together with their disciples.
Yet, those who are wise and virtuous rely on their own cleverness and fail to believe that they are originally unborn, originally empty, originally pure, and originally complete. On the contrary—
Desiring to augment their intelligence and broaden their knowledge and vision, yet unaware that they would ultimately enter the cycle of birth and death,
I am thus compelled to further instruct sentient beings regarding the path of mindfulness of the Buddha. I declare that in the West dwells Amitābha Buddha,
who has made a vow to welcome and guide those who practice mindfulness of the Buddha, so that they may together return to the Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss.
Once born in the Pure Land, one may also temporarily escape the suffering of saṃsāric birth and death.

At some future time, one will draw near to the Buddha’s light and personally realize non-arising; this is certain. Therefore, there are scriptures such as the *Mahā-amitābha-sūtra* and the *Sukhāvatī-vyūha-sūtra*.

What we recite during our evening practice today is the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra*, which describes birth through transformation within a lotus flower—this is not comparable to [other modes of rebirth].

Though of ordinary substance within the womb, all that is heard is the Buddha’s speech, and all that is seen is the Buddha’s work. Since the Land of Ultimate Bliss has nothing with which it can be compared, how could these be words intended to deceive people?
The Buddha said: "If I were deceiving people, I would, on their behalf, undergo the sufferings of sentient beings for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges."
The suffering of the Hell of the Plucked Tongue—how could this be a minor matter? How then could the Buddha dare to deceive people?

It is because whenever the Buddha enters meditative concentration (*samādhi*), he fully accepts invitations from all ten directions to preach the Dharma in the heavens, hells, dragon palaces, ocean treasuries, and every other place;
thus, he travels to assemblies before Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. How much more so for Amitābha Buddha, who would not fail to do so?

Indeed, it is so. Therefore, the Buddha specifically expounded this in detail; these are the ultimate words of the Buddha. It is only for those ordinary people with squinting eyes that one cannot speak of them.
Alas! How could there be a matter concerning the appearance of a Great Sage in the world that can be discussed with ordinary people?
A Letter to the Monk Sengruzheng of the Seclusion Retreat Yesterday, when I met with Crown Prince Qian’an, he spoke at length about my teacher, Ruzheng.
He said that from his youth, Ruzheng has been extraordinary; now, having closed himself in retreat for three years, he is truly one who practices for the sake of life and destiny.

It is a pity that our dwellings are so far apart, preventing me from frequently visiting his door to inquire after him. Generally speaking, although there are many schools among those who study the Buddha-dharma, [End of excerpt]
There are only two kinds. What are these two? First, the recitation of the Buddha’s name (nien-fo); second, the practice of Zen (can-ch’an). In Zen, one seeks to see one's own Buddha;
seeing one's own Buddha, one immediately attains Buddhahood oneself. However, those of shallow capacity mostly lack sufficient faith.

Because they lack faith, their vision does not penetrate to the core—this is what is meant by "passing it by in plain sight. As for the recitation of the Buddha’s name, one seeks to see that [Buddha].
Amitābha Buddha. Upon seeing that Buddha, one shall depart forever for the Buddha-land;
daily hearing the Buddha’s voice and daily witnessing the Buddha’s deeds, one will ultimately see one’s own Buddha and become one’s own Buddha.

Compared to those who attain Buddhahood through Zen meditation, although the speed differs, the goal of becoming one’s own Buddha is the same. It is likewise the means to escape the cycle of birth and death.
...of suffering. It is also one in that they are not encompassed by any of the realms of existence, whether heavenly, hellish, or otherwise, whether good or evil.
This is because Amitābha Buddha has made a vow to receive all sentient beings who practice mindfulness of him and lead them to be born together in the Pure Land.

Thus he said: "Sentient beings may come to an end, but my vow shall never cease; so long as there remains even a single sentient being who has not attained Buddhahood, [I shall not enter parinirvāṇa]."
One attains *nirvāṇa* therein. Now, it is evident that if sentient beings have no end to their exhaustion, then the Buddha’s vows likewise have no end to their fulfillment.
Such are the Buddha’s vows; therefore, to claim that the Buddha is unwilling to receive and guide me is impossible.

It is only that sentient beings in this world have heavy habitual tendencies and thick bonds of affection; they do not believe in the Buddha themselves, they are unwilling to go themselves, and they do not [seek help] themselves.
Listen to his guidance. Although the Buddha has made vows, what can he do for sentient beings?

Now, since you have single-mindedly placed your faith in the Buddha and single-mindedly recited his name, why worry that you will not be born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss? Once born in the Land of Ultimate Bliss, you will take refuge in your parents;
what hells, heavens, or other realms could then dare to falsely summon and seize you? Please reflect upon this with a virtuous mind.

If you can recite them with focused mindfulness, At the time of death, we shall walk hand-in-hand together.
Namo Amitābha Buddha. This is my passport to the West;
when reciting it, let the words flow naturally from the mouth. When walking, take the path with confident steps.
Namo Amitābha Buddha. Passing through the net of earth and the net of heaven.
Seeing this body as still being that of a sentient being, The body to come shall be Amitābha.
*Namu Amida Butsu*. There is no need for flowery words or clever speech;
If I truly practice mindfulness of the Buddha, The Buddha will then preach the Dharma for me.
Namo Amitābha Buddha! Call out His name with every voice, so that He who is compassionate and great in compassion may save all suffering beings.
Because of His great compassion, may His vows not fail.
Namo Amitābha Buddha! May I realize the fruit of enlightenment in this very life.
Just recite "Namu Amida Butsu" once, and a single lotus flower will naturally emerge.
I am the descendant of that family;
do not worry that he will not answer when called, but only worry that I do not go to his door.
Homage to Amitābha Buddha. He is the ancestral patriarch of my house;
if one can recite His name with a sincere heart, one will forever escape the suffering realms of saṃsāra and be certain to attain the Pure Land. (End)
